title: Net balances and debt simplification
idea: Simplifying debts replaces the web of who-owes-whom with one net balance per person, then has the largest debtor pay the largest creditor until everyone reaches zero.

analogy.text: Chips at the end of a card night. Nobody repays each hand; each player cashes out their final chip count.
analogy.breaks: There is no central bank here; debtors pay creditors directly.

points: A user's net balance is everything they paid minus every share they owe.
Nets always sum to zero; any other sum means an expense was recorded wrongly.
Each greedy transfer zeroes someone, so n people need at most n − 1.
Greedy is not always minimal; finding the true minimum is NP-hard in general.

hero.title: Greedy settlement of four net balances

steps.caption: Start from net balances in cents. Ben paid 6000 and owes 6000 in shares, so Ben is already settled.
Pick the largest debtor and the largest creditor: Chen and Asha.
Chen pays the smaller of the two amounts. Chen reaches zero; Asha is still owed 1000.
Repeat with what is left: Dev is the only debtor, Asha the only creditor.
Dev pays 1000 and both reach zero in the same transfer.
Every transfer zeroed at least one person. Compare this with the pairwise list in the first example.

code.title: The problem: pairwise debts
code.caption: Three expenses settled pair by pair, then the same data reduced to one net number per person.

walk.text: Three expenses. Shares come from a split strategy, so each already sums to its total.
Each share becomes a debt from that user to the payer. Your own share is skipped.
Settling pair by pair needs one transfer per entry, including cycles like Asha and Dev.
The net view keeps one number per person: the payer gains each share, each user loses their own.
Nets sum to zero. Money moves between people; it is never created or lost.

code.title: The fix: net and settle
code.caption: A `BalanceSheet` keeps net balances and settles them greedily with two priority queues.

walk.text: One `long` per user. A `TreeMap` keeps printing and iteration order stable.
Recording costs O(shares · log users) with a TreeMap. Inputs are checked first; bad calls change nothing.
The invariant check: if nets do not sum to zero, settling would be wrong.
Two max-heaps. Ties break by name, so the same input always gives the same transfers.
The largest debtor pays the largest creditor the smaller of their two amounts.
Whoever is not at zero goes back in the queue with what remains.
Each loop zeroes at least one person, so there are at most n − 1 transfers.

pitfalls: Keeping only pairwise debts preserves cycles, such as Asha owing Dev while Dev owes Asha.
Settling from a `HashMap` or `Map.of` without tie-breaks leaves transfer order unspecified.
Storing balances apart from expenses lets them drift; update both in one place.

quiz.q: Same `BalanceSheet` as the fix. What does this print?
options: Transfer[from=C, to=B, cents=500] then Transfer[from=B, to=A, cents=500]
Transfer[from=B, to=A, cents=500] then Transfer[from=C, to=A, cents=500]
quiz.why: B is owed 500 by C and owes 500 to A, so B nets to zero. Only C (−1000) and A (+1000) remain: one transfer.

takeaway: Net each person to one number, then match biggest debtor with biggest creditor.

starters: Can you show a case where greedy settlement is not the minimum?
Should balances be computed on demand or updated on every expense?
How would simplifying debts work across several groups at once?
